dataset: Mission Architect In-Game Educational Guide & 30s Demo Storyboard

explanations.shortExplanation: A rocket can push far less mass to the Moon than to low Earth orbit: the trans-lunar injection burn needs about 3.1 km/s more after orbit. SLS Block 1 sends over 27 t to the Moon, a Falcon 9-class rocket only a few tonnes.
explanations.tradeOffTip: Every part you add has to fit under the rocket's Moon payload. If the stack is too heavy, drop a part you do not need or pay for a bigger rocket.
explanations.sourceLabel: NASA — Space Launch System Core Stage

explanations.shortExplanation: A rocket throws away empty tanks and engines as it climbs, so the next stage only pushes what is still useful. That is why every real Moon rocket has two or more stages plus boosters.
explanations.tradeOffTip: If a stage runs dry before orbit, the vehicle is too heavy for that rocket: lighten the spacecraft or pick the bigger rocket.
explanations.formula: dv_total = sum over stages of Isp_i * g0 * ln(m0_i / mf_i)
explanations.sourceLabel: NASA Glenn Research Center — Booster Staging

explanations.shortExplanation: Delta-v is how much a spacecraft can change its speed with the propellant it carries. It grows only with the logarithm of the mass ratio, so extra fuel buys less and less.
explanations.tradeOffTip: Course corrections and the trip home come out of the service module's delta-v. A larger service module gives margin, but it is heavier for the rocket.
explanations.sourceLabel: NASA Glenn Research Center — Ideal Rocket Equation

explanations.shortExplanation: From the parking orbit, one burn (trans-lunar injection) raises the far point of the orbit to the Moon's distance. Timed right, the Moon's gravity swings the spacecraft round its far side and back to Earth without another big burn, as on Artemis II.
explanations.tradeOffTip: Burn too early or too late and the Moon is not there when you arrive. Fire when the Moon is the right angle ahead, and keep propellant for the small corrections.

explanations.shortExplanation: The crew needs oxygen, water and carbon dioxide removal for every day of the flight. The life support system carries a fixed number of days; a slower trip uses them up.
explanations.tradeOffTip: Plan for the days the flight really takes, plus a margin for a late return, not just the nominal mission length.
explanations.sourceLabel: NASA — Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS)

explanations.shortExplanation: Coming back from the Moon the capsule hits the air at about 11 km/s, much faster than from low orbit (about 7.8 km/s). The heat shield takes the heat and the angle of entry sets how hard the crew is pressed into their seats.
explanations.tradeOffTip: Too steep and the g-load and heating are dangerous; too shallow and the capsule skips off the atmosphere. Course corrections on the way home aim for the narrow corridor.
explanations.formula: Energy per kg = v^2 / 2  (about 60 MJ/kg at 11 km/s)

explanations.shortExplanation: Solar flares and coronal mass ejections can send bursts of energetic protons. Near Earth the magnetic field deflects them; on the way to the Moon nothing does.
explanations.tradeOffTip: The events in the game are real ones from NASA's DONKI database. The dangerous ones are the proton events (NOAA S-scale), not only a high Kp.
explanations.formula: S = floor(log10(proton flux in pfu)), from 10 pfu (S1)
explanations.sourceLabel: NASA CCMC DONKI Space Weather Database

explanations.shortExplanation: Orion has no heavy shielding everywhere, so during a solar particle event the crew builds a dense shelter with the stowage bags on board and waits inside.
explanations.tradeOffTip: Fit the radiation shelter for deep space flights. Without it, a strong storm outside the magnetosphere gives the crew a dangerous dose.
explanations.formula: Safe = inside magnetosphere OR flux < 10 pfu OR shelter fitted
